Exercise A

Comparing precisely

B2 comparing goes beyond -er and more: use modifiers (far, considerably, a lot), twice as … as, the least, and the more …, the more …. Choose the correct form for each gap.

Before you start — optional, not marked
This is just to get you thinking. You can leave it empty and it does not count towards your score.
Twelve moments from a flat search

1. Rent in the centre is 1 higher than in the suburbs: almost €150 more a month.

2. The new flat is not nearly 2 noisy as the old one.

3. Of the three flats we saw, this is by far 3 best option for a group.

4. The 4 I think about it, the less convinced I am.

5. Flat B costs twice 5 much as Flat A.

6. Of the three, Flat A is the 6 convenient for the university.

7. Living with flatmates is 7 stressful than I had expected.

8. Flat A is in one of the 8 parts of the city.

9. Rents are rising 9 than wages, so students are struggling.

10. The more flats we saw, 10 we liked the first one.

11. By the time we reached the second flat, someone had already 11 it.

12. Would it be possible 12 see Flat B once more before we decide?

Exercise B

Choose the flat

Breakout rooms, 20 minutes. Each person gets a role with private priorities. Speak English only. You must agree on one flat, and nobody gets everything they want. Then each person types the group’s result here.

The three flats

Flat A: €420 a month · 30 minutes to the university by tram · very quiet · two flatmates · 45 m² · balcony.

Flat B: €560 a month · 5 minutes on foot · noisy (bars downstairs) · no flatmates · 22 m².

Flat C: €480 a month · 15 minutes by bike · lively street · three flatmates · 60 m² · big shared kitchen.

Use at least four comparing structures from Exercise A while you negotiate (far less …, by far the …, not nearly as … as, twice as … as, the more …, the more …).

Word count: 0

Write 90–130 words in the group’s decision. Say which flat you chose, compare it with the others, and show where someone gave way (We agreed on … even though … was far cheaper).
